Early consideration of physical therapy and shared decision-making regarding corticosteroid injection if inflammatory capsulitis is confirmed.

This 2-month history of gradual-onset, nocturnal left shoulder pain with progressive global restriction in active and passive range of motion (forward flexion, abduction, external and internal rotation all markedly limited and painful) is highly characteristic of *adhesive capsulitis* (frozen shoulder). The absence of neurologic symptoms (no radicular pain, weakness, numbness), negative red flags for malignancy/infection/systemic illness, and lack of trauma or acute onset further support a primary capsular process over rotator cuff tear (which typically shows greater active than passive ROM loss) or cervical radiculopathy (which would present with dermatomal symptoms or positive Spurling’s/upper limb tension tests). While rotator cuff tendinopathy or early glenohumeral osteoarthritis remain in the differential, the *symmetrical, global capsular pattern* — especially the profound loss of internal rotation (to only 15°, far below functional level) and near-identical active/passive deficits — is the hallmark of adhesive capsulitis. Notably, adhesive capsulitis commonly presents with severe sleep disturbance due to capsular stretch at night, and it classically evolves through painful, stiff, and thawing phases — consistent with this subacute (2-month) presentation.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Adhesive capsulitis
